4.4.Epilogue: existence of sections and2–sections.Lefschetz fibrations without sections appear
to be rare to the authors of this article. The obstructionω(f)∈Ggives a concrete way to prove that
a section does not exist, but using it requires detecting nontriviality in the nonabelian groupG=F/N,
and in practice the calculation can be costly. Thus it is useful to know where to look for good candidates.
The discussion in Section 2.3 suggests one source. In constructions obtained by breeding lower-
genus relations, boundary components often record sections before the relevant capping and cancellation
operations are performed. Surviving boundary components give honest sections, while cancellations
of boundary twists that hold only after forgetting the marked point may leave residual point-pushing
terms. When no boundary component survives to give an obvious section, and the abelianized obstruction
vanishes, the resulting fibration is a natural candidate for the nonabelian obstruction, as in the examples
considered above. The genus–7 calculation reinforces this picture, and we expect that the higher-genus

Question 21.Does every Lefschetz fibration overS 2 admit a2–section?
By Theorem 6, this question is equivalent to asking whether the divisibilitym(f) of the fiber class
always divides 2. In particular, it would follow from the stronger assertion that the fiber class of every
Lefschetz fibration overS 2 is primitive. This primitivity assertion was claimed in [35], but the proof
contains a gap; see the appendix of [3]. We do not know whether the assertion itself is true. For achiral
Lefschetz fibrations, however, the analogous statement is false: Gompf’s examples show that one cannot
expect such low-degree multisections without the positivity assumption on the singularities [14].

We still believe that Lefschetz fibrations over the 2–sphere without sections are very rare, and with
this in mind, our counter-examples raise many questions about how special the topology of their total
spaces is. In light of Corollary 19, we ask:
Question 22.Can a closed aspherical4–manifold admit a Lefschetz fibration overS 2?
We do not know whether the original genus–9 total spaceX=X 1 is aspherical, even though it does
not admit a strictly negative sectional curvature by 17. Its untwisted self fiber sumsX n, however, are not
aspherical forn≥2. Indeed, sincewis central and has infinite order inG, the quotientπ 1(Xn) =G/⟨w n⟩
contains the cyclic subgroup⟨w⟩/⟨w n⟩ ∼= Zn. This rules out asphericity, since the fundamental group of
a closed aspherical manifold is torsion-free [18, Proposition 2.45].
Specifically, it would be interesting to know if a hyperbolic 4–manifold could admit a Lefschetz fibra-
tion; cf. [2, Problem 4.95(a)].
